subtopics.title: Charges Must Cancel — the One Law of Formula Writing

questions.question: The one law governing every ionic formula is:
options: The compound must be electrically neutral — total positive and negative charges cancel
Every formula needs exactly two elements

questions.question: A group two metal like calcium forms an ion with charge:
Why does magnesium chloride need TWO chlorides (MgCl2)?
options: One Cl⁻ cannot cancel Mg's 2+ charge, but two can

subtopics.title: Calcium Chloride and the Crossover Method

questions.question: The formula for calcium chloride is:
In the crossover method, the numbers that cross over are:
options: The sizes of the charges, each becoming the OTHER ion's subscript

questions.question: Crossing Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ gives Mg2O2. The correct final formula is:
options: MgO — subscripts must be simplified to the smallest ratio
Mg2O2 — the crossover result is always final

questions.question: The charge audit for CaCl2 confirms neutrality because:
options: One Ca at 2+ gives +2 and two Cl at 1− give −2, summing to zero
Calcium and chlorine are in the same period

subtopics.title: Ammonium Sulphate — Polyatomic Ions and the Bracket Rule

questions.question: The ammonium and sulphate ions are:
The formula for ammonium sulphate is:
Brackets are required in (NH4)2SO4 because:
options: The subscript 2 must multiply the whole ammonium team — without brackets the formula miscounts atoms
Sulphate demands brackets around its partner
Brackets make the formula look neater

subtopics.title: Iron(III) Oxide — Roman Numerals and the Complete Method

questions.question: The Roman numeral in 'iron(III) oxide' tells you:
options: The iron ion carries a 3+ charge
It is the third oxide discovered

questions.question: The formula for iron(III) oxide is:
Why do transition metals like iron need Roman numerals when group one metals do not?
options: Transition metals can form more than one ion (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺), so the name must specify which
Group one metals have no charge
It is a historical accident with no meaning

questions.question: Iron(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide are:
options: Different compounds — FeO and Fe2O3 — with different properties
The same compound written two ways
